title: Blood family only at Thanksgiving
author: Storytime
hook: My mother-in-law announced Thanksgiving is blood family only this year. No spouses. So my husband made his own announcement.
story: My husband's family is big. Four kids, all married, eight grandkids. Every year, Thanksgiving is at his mom Linda's house. Last week, Linda sent a group text. This year, I want it to be just my children and grandchildren. Blood family only. Spouses can spend the day with their own families. I've been married to her son for nine years. My kids are her grandkids. I didn't say anything. I just handed my phone to my husband, Chris. He read it, then typed one message in the group chat. Spouses and anyone else who's been uninvited, come to our house instead. Turkey's on me. Within an hour, all four spouses said yes. Then something I didn't expect. His sister replied, we're coming too. Then his younger brother. Then the other sister. Every single one of Linda's kids chose to come to our house. With their spouses. And their kids. Linda will be alone with her husband. This morning, she called Chris crying. She says she was only trying to have one special day with her children. She asked if she can come to our Thanksgiving. Should we let her?
caption: blood family only backfired 🦃 #storytime
sound: a tense family drama piano that softens at the end at very low volume
why: In-laws excluding spouses at Thanksgiving is trending this week, the husband's response is satisfying, the siblings' choice escalates it, and should we let her in splits viewers.

title: Brother-in-law leaves before cleanup
author: Storytime
hook: Every Thanksgiving, my brother-in-law leaves right before the dishes. Last year, I followed him.
story: I've hosted Thanksgiving for six years. My wife and I cook for twenty people. And every year, right when the plates come off the table, my brother-in-law Kevin stands up and says, well, I better get going. He never helps. Not one dish. Not one trash bag. My wife says to let it go. I couldn't. So last year, when he left, I told everyone I was getting ice, and I followed him. He drove twenty minutes to the other side of town. He parked outside a small apartment building and went in with two huge bags. Through the window, I saw him. He was in a tiny apartment with an old man in a wheelchair. Setting the table. Serving turkey. They were laughing. I went back home and asked my wife's mom about it. She went quiet. Then she told me. That old man is Kevin's former foster dad. The one who raised him for six years before the family adopted him. He has no one else. Kevin's been bringing him dinner every Thanksgiving for twelve years. He's never told anyone. This year, should I invite them both to our table?
caption: he wasn't skipping the dishes 🍽️ #storytime
sound: a warm, quiet piano that swells gently at very low volume
why: Guests who skip cleanup are a trending Thanksgiving complaint, following him builds suspense, the foster dad twist is deeply emotional, and the invite question invites heartfelt comments.

title: Still at the kids table at thirty-four
author: Storytime
hook: I'm thirty-four, and my grandma still seats me at the kids' table every Thanksgiving. This year, I found out why.
story: Every Thanksgiving at my grandma's house, there's the grown up table and the kids' table. The kids' table is tiny, plastic, in the living room. I'm thirty-four. I have a job, a mortgage, a beard. And every year, my name card is at the kids' table, next to my seven year old cousins. My aunts think it's hilarious. Last year, I finally asked my grandma why. She took my hand and said, sit there one more time, and keep your ears open. So I did. And for the first time, I listened. From the grown up table, I heard everything. My aunt arguing about who gets grandma's house. My uncle complaining about how much her care costs. My mom saying she'd sell the ring the second grandma was gone. Grandma heard it too. She sat at the head of that table every year, smiling, and listening. After dinner, she came over, sat down on a tiny plastic chair next to me, and said, now you know why I keep you here. You're the only one who never asks me for anything. Then she handed me an envelope. And told me not to open it until Christmas. Part two?
caption: the kids table was protection 🥧 #storytime
sound: a gentle, slightly ominous music box at very low volume
why: The kids' table is a classic Thanksgiving joke that's trending again, the grown ups' conversation reveals family greed, grandma's reason is a powerful twist, and the envelope sets up a part two.
